issues: The forecast that Damascus's riches and Samaria's spoil will be taken is summarized accurately, but its phrasing as what will happen “before the child can say” is a paraphrase rather than the verse's exact wording. No future conquest should be depicted as a present scene.

The Lord is explicitly said to speak again in verse 5, but verse 6 does not explicitly identify the speaker of these words; attributing the quoted verse 6 text directly to the Lord is a reasonable contextual inference, not an explicit attribution.

Verse 8 says the king will pass through Judah and overflow it, but the summary calls the land “the land” and specifies “the king” as the one reaching to the neck; preserve the verse’s metaphorical wording and do not stage it as a literal flood or present event.

The speech in verses 9–10 is not explicitly attributed to the Lord; labeling the dialogue speaker as the Lord is unsupported. “Broken in pieces” and the counsel’s failure are prophetic statements, not present-tense events.

Verses 11–13 identify the Lord as speaking and instructing the speaker, but the quoted lines omit intervening wording; the excerpts themselves are exact and contiguous. Do not render “with a strong hand” as a visible hand.

Verse 14 does not explicitly identify the speaker of the quoted words. The stone, rock, and snare language is figurative; verse 15’s predicted stumbling and capture should not be staged as a present event.

Verse 16 gives the command without explicitly naming its speaker; attributing it to the Lord is a contextual inference. Verse 17 says the Lord hides his face, but this is not a description of a visible appearance.

Verse 19 reports what people will say, then gives a question, but does not explicitly identify the question’s speaker; assigning it to the Lord is unsupported. Verse 20 gives the law-and-testimony statement without explicit speaker attribution. Do not stage the reported advice or spirits as a present encounter.
